PSE II · Chapter 28

Magnetic Fields

Forces on moving charge & their sources

← PSE II Course

28.0 — A Force Unlike Any Other

Every force we have studied so far — gravitational, electric, elastic — acts along a line connecting the interacting objects. This chapter introduces a force that breaks that pattern entirely. The magnetic force acts perpendicular to a charged particle’s motion — it bends trajectories without changing speed.

The story begins with the Chinese polymath Shen Kuo (1031–1095), who described the magnetic compass and its use for navigation in 1088. The mathematical explanation arrived only in 1820, when Hans Christian Ørsted (1777–1851) noticed during a lecture that a current-carrying wire deflected a nearby compass needle — electricity and magnetism were connected. Within months, Jean-Baptiste Biot and Félix Savart had quantified the magnetic field of a wire, and André-Marie Ampère showed that current-carrying wires exert forces on each other.

“I was almost in doubt about the thing; however, I remember that I thought the effect was so evident that it would be inexplicable to interrupt the lecture to investigate more closely.” — Hans Christian Ørsted, 1820

You have already seen in Chapter 31 that light is an electromagnetic wave traveling at \(c = 1/\sqrt{\mu_0\varepsilon_0}\). This chapter explains the “magnetic” half of that story — where \(\vec{B}\) comes from, what it does, and why \(\mu_0\) appears in the speed of light.

*Personal note: Ørsted’s discovery is one of the great “accidental” moments in physics. But it was accidental only in timing — he had been searching for a connection between electricity and magnetism for years. The prepared mind recognizes what the unprepared mind overlooks.

28.1 — The Magnetic Field

In Chapter 22, we defined the electric field \(\vec{E}\) by placing a test charge at rest and measuring the force. The magnetic field \(\vec{B}\) requires a subtler procedure: a stationary charge feels no magnetic force. We must fire a moving charge through the region and observe the deflection. The field is whatever explains that deflection via the force law developed in Section 28.2.

The SI unit is the tesla (T): \(1\ \text{T} = 1\ \text{N}/(\text{A}\cdot\text{m})\).

Source Approximate \(B\)
Earth’s surface \(50\ \mu\text{T}\)
Refrigerator magnet \(5\ \text{mT}\)
MRI machine \(1.5\)–\(3\ \text{T}\)
Strongest lab magnets \(\sim 45\ \text{T}\)

Earth’s field is remarkably weak — about 100,000 times weaker than an MRI magnet — yet strong enough to align a compass needle. This tells you something about how sensitive magnetized materials can be.

Electric Field vs. Magnetic Field

The most important conceptual distinction in this chapter:

Property Electric Field \(\vec{E}\) (Ch 22) Magnetic Field \(\vec{B}\) (Ch 28)
Source Stationary or moving charge Moving charge / current
Force on charge \(q\) \(\vec{F} = q\vec{E}\) (along \(\vec{E}\)) \(\vec{F} = q\vec{v}\times\vec{B}\) (\(\perp\) to \(\vec{v}\) and \(\vec{B}\))
Force on stationary charge? Yes No
Does work on charge? Yes No (\(\vec{F}\perp\vec{v}\) always)
Field lines Begin on \(+\), end on \(-\) Always closed loops
Gauss’s Law \(\oint \vec{E}\cdot d\vec{A} = Q_\text{enc}/\varepsilon_0\) \(\oint \vec{B}\cdot d\vec{A} = 0\)

Electric field lines begin on positive charges and terminate on negative charges. Magnetic field lines form closed loops. There are no magnetic charges — no “magnetic monopoles” — from which field lines could originate. This asymmetry is encoded in Gauss’s Law for magnetism (Section 28.7): \(\oint \vec{B}\cdot d\vec{A} = 0\).

28.2 — The Lorentz Force — Motion in Magnetic Fields

The Magnetic Force on a Moving Charge

A particle with charge \(q\) moving with velocity \(\vec{v}\) in a magnetic field \(\vec{B}\) experiences a force:

\[\boxed{\vec{F} = q\vec{v}\times\vec{B}}\]

This is the magnetic component of the Lorentz force. (The full Lorentz force, \(\vec{F} = q\vec{E} + q\vec{v}\times\vec{B}\), includes both electric and magnetic contributions.) The magnitude is \(F = |q|vB\sin\theta\), where \(\theta\) is the angle between \(\vec{v}\) and \(\vec{B}\). The direction follows the right-hand rule: point fingers along \(\vec{v}\), curl toward \(\vec{B}\), and your thumb gives \(\vec{F}\) for a positive charge. Three critical observations:

  1. \(\vec{v}\parallel\vec{B}\) (\(\theta = 0°\) or \(180°\)): \(F = 0\). A charge moving along the field feels no force.
  2. \(\vec{v}\perp\vec{B}\) (\(\theta = 90°\)): \(F = |q|vB\), the maximum force.
  3. Always: \(\vec{F}\perp\vec{v}\). The magnetic force does no work: \(W = \int\vec{F}\cdot\vec{v}\,dt = 0\).

The third point is profound. The magnetic force changes the direction of motion but never the speed or kinetic energy. Compare this to Chapter 22: a charged particle in uniform \(\vec{E}\) experienced constant acceleration \(\rightarrow\) parabolic trajectory. Here, constant deflection \(\perp\) to velocity \(\rightarrow\) circular trajectory. One changes speed; the other changes direction.

Circular Motion in a Uniform Magnetic Field

Consider a positive charge \(q\) moving with speed \(v\) perpendicular to a uniform \(\vec{B}\) (into the page). At every instant, \(\vec{F} = q\vec{v}\times\vec{B}\) points toward the center of curvature — it is a centripetal force. Setting magnetic force equal to centripetal force:

\[|q|vB = \frac{mv^2}{r} \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad \boxed{r = \frac{mv}{|q|B}}\]

This is the cyclotron radius. Faster particles orbit in larger circles; stronger fields produce tighter orbits. The cyclotron frequency follows from \(v = 2\pi r f\):

\[\boxed{f = \frac{|q|B}{2\pi m}} \qquad T = \frac{1}{f} = \frac{2\pi m}{|q|B}\]

The frequency is independent of speed. A fast particle orbits in a larger circle but covers it faster — the two effects cancel exactly. This is why the cyclotron works: particles of a given \(q/m\) all orbit at the same frequency, so a single oscillating electric field can accelerate them repeatedly. When \(\vec{v}\) has a component parallel to \(\vec{B}\), the parallel component is unaffected while the perpendicular component drives circular motion, producing a helix — the mechanism behind the aurora borealis. The Lorentz force also deflects charge carriers sideways inside a conductor, producing a transverse voltage called the Hall effect, used to measure \(B\) fields.

Example: Proton in a Magnetic Field

A proton (\(m = 1.67\times10^{-27}\ \text{kg}\), \(q = 1.60\times10^{-19}\ \text{C}\)) moves at \(v = 8.0\times10^{6}\ \text{m/s}\) perpendicular to \(B = 0.30\ \text{T}\).

(A) \(r = mv/(|q|B) = (1.67\times10^{-27})(8.0\times10^{6})/[(1.60\times10^{-19})(0.30)] = \boxed{0.28\ \text{m}}\)

(B) \(f = |q|B/(2\pi m) = (1.60\times10^{-19})(0.30)/[2\pi(1.67\times10^{-27})] = \boxed{4.6\ \text{MHz}}\)

(C) \(T = 1/f = \boxed{0.22\ \mu\text{s}}\)

Interpretation: The proton completes nearly 5 million orbits per second in a circle roughly the size of a basketball. Doubling the speed would double the radius but leave the frequency unchanged — faster particles simply take wider paths at the same rate.

28.3 — Force on a Current-Carrying Conductor

From Single Charge to Bulk Current

A current-carrying wire in a magnetic field experiences a force because each mobile carrier inside feels \(q\vec{v}_d\times\vec{B}\). Consider a segment \(d\vec{\ell}\) carrying current \(I\). The number of carriers is \(nA\,d\ell\) (carrier density \(n\), cross-sectional area \(A\)); each feels force \(q\vec{v}_d\times\vec{B}\). The total force is proportional to \(nAqv_d\) — which, from Chapter 26, equals \(I\). So:

\[\boxed{d\vec{F} = I\,d\vec{\ell}\times\vec{B}}\]

For a straight wire of length \(L\) in a uniform field:

\[\boxed{\vec{F} = I\vec{L}\times\vec{B}} \qquad F = BIL\sin\theta\]

This is not a new law — it is \(\vec{F} = q\vec{v}\times\vec{B}\) applied to \(\sim 10^{23}\) carriers simultaneously.

Example: Force on a Wire

A wire of length \(L = 0.50\ \text{m}\) carries \(I = 2.0\ \text{A}\) in the \(+x\) direction. \(\vec{B} = 0.080\,\hat{z}\ \text{T}\).

\[\vec{F} = I\vec{L}\times\vec{B} = (2.0)(0.50)\,\hat{x}\times(0.080)\,\hat{z}\]

Since \(\hat{x}\times\hat{z} = -\hat{y}\): \(\vec{F} = \boxed{-0.080\,\hat{y}\ \text{N}}\)

About the weight of a single sheet of paper — but the same physics drives industrial electric motors producing thousands of horsepower.

28.4 — Torque on a Current Loop and the Magnetic Dipole

The Rectangular Loop in a Uniform Field

Consider a rectangular loop (width \(a\), height \(b\), area \(A = ab\)) carrying current \(I\) in uniform \(\vec{B}\). Using \(\vec{F} = I\vec{L}\times\vec{B}\) on each side: sides parallel to \(\vec{B}\) feel zero force; sides perpendicular feel equal and opposite forces (\(F = BIb\)), forming a couple — zero net force, nonzero torque. When the loop’s normal \(\hat{n}\) makes angle \(\theta\) with \(\vec{B}\), the torque is \(\tau = BIA\sin\theta\). For \(N\) turns:

\[\boxed{\tau = NIAB\sin\theta}\]

The Magnetic Dipole Moment

We define the magnetic dipole moment: \(\boxed{\vec{\mu} = NIA\hat{n}}\), where \(\hat{n}\) follows the right-hand rule (curl fingers with current, thumb = \(\hat{n}\)). The SI unit is A·m². The torque and potential energy take elegant vector forms:

\[\boxed{\vec{\tau} = \vec{\mu}\times\vec{B}} \qquad \boxed{U = -\vec{\mu}\cdot\vec{B} = -\mu B\cos\theta}\]

Stable equilibrium at \(\theta = 0\) (\(\vec{\mu}\parallel\vec{B}\), minimum \(U\)); unstable at \(\theta = 180°\).

The Grand Analogy — Electric Dipole Meets Magnetic Dipole

Every formula has an exact structural counterpart:

Property Electric Dipole \(\vec{p}\) (Ch 25) Magnetic Dipole \(\vec{\mu}\) (Ch 28)
Definition \(\vec{p} = q\vec{d}\) \(\vec{\mu} = NIA\hat{n}\)
Torque in field \(\vec{\tau} = \vec{p}\times\vec{E}\) \(\vec{\tau} = \vec{\mu}\times\vec{B}\)
Potential energy \(U = -\vec{p}\cdot\vec{E}\) \(U = -\vec{\mu}\cdot\vec{B}\)
Stable equilibrium \(\vec{p}\parallel\vec{E}\) \(\vec{\mu}\parallel\vec{B}\)
Physical origin Charge separation Current loop

The loop acts like a compass needle: \(\vec{\mu}\) aligns with \(\vec{B}\) at equilibrium. A bar magnet’s field arises from aligned atomic magnetic dipole moments — each atom is a tiny current loop. A DC motor exploits this: a current loop on an axle with a commutator (split ring reversing current every half-turn) ensures continuous rotation. Every motor from a hair dryer to a Tesla is this physics at scale.

Example: Torque on a Coil

A 200-turn square coil (side \(\ell = 5.0\ \text{cm}\)) carries \(I = 0.80\ \text{A}\) in a field \(B = 0.35\ \text{T}\).

(A) \(\mu = NIA = (200)(0.80)(0.050)^2 = \boxed{0.40\ \text{A}\cdot\text{m}^2}\)

(B) \(\tau_\text{max} = \mu B = (0.40)(0.35) = \boxed{0.14\ \text{N}\cdot\text{m}}\)

(C) \(U_{90°} = 0\); \(U_{0°} = -\mu B = \boxed{-0.14\ \text{J}}\). The coil releases 0.14 J swinging from 90° to alignment — this is what drives a motor shaft each quarter-turn.

28.5 — Sources of Magnetic Fields — The Biot-Savart Law

Every Current Creates a Magnetic Field

Sections 28.2–28.4 answered: given \(\vec{B}\), what force does it exert? We now ask the complementary question: given a current, what \(\vec{B}\) does it create? The answer was established by Biot and Savart in 1820. The Biot-Savart Law gives the infinitesimal field at point P due to a current element \(I\,d\vec{\ell}\):

\[\boxed{d\vec{B} = \frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{I\,d\vec{\ell}\times\hat{r}}{r^2}}\]

where \(\mu_0 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \text{T}\cdot\text{m/A}\) is the permeability of free space, \(d\vec{\ell}\) points along the current, \(\hat{r}\) points from element to field point, and \(r\) is the distance. Total field: \(\vec{B} = \int d\vec{B}\).

Structural Parallel — Biot-Savart and Coulomb

Property Coulomb’s Law (Ch 22) Biot-Savart Law (Ch 28)
Source Point charge \(dq\) Current element \(I\,d\vec{\ell}\)
Field \(d\vec{E} = k_e\,dq\,\hat{r}/r^2\) \(d\vec{B} = (\mu_0/4\pi)\,I\,d\vec{\ell}\times\hat{r}/r^2\)
Direction Along \(\hat{r}\) (radial) \(\perp\) to both \(d\vec{\ell}\) and \(\hat{r}\)
\(1/r^2\) dependence Yes Yes

The key difference: \(\vec{E}\) points radially outward; \(\vec{B}\) circulates around the wire. This is why magnetic field lines form loops rather than radiating outward.

Field of an Infinite Straight Wire

Integrating the Biot-Savart Law along an infinite wire (the same integration-along-a-line technique used for charged rods in Chapter 23):

\[\boxed{B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}}\]

The field circulates around the wire in closed circles, with direction given by the right-hand rule: thumb along current, fingers curl in the direction of \(\vec{B}\).

The \(1/r\) dependence — not \(1/r^2\) — matches the electric field of an infinite line charge (\(E = \lambda/2\pi\varepsilon_0 r\) from Ch 23). The slower falloff reflects the 1D source geometry: every point along the infinite wire contributes.

Field on the Axis of a Circular Loop

For a loop of radius \(R\) carrying current \(I\), the on-axis field at distance \(x\) from center:

\[\boxed{B = \frac{\mu_0 I R^2}{2(R^2 + x^2)^{3/2}}}\]

Figure 28.6: Magnetic field of a circular current loop. Left: On-axis field. Right: Field lines — every line is a closed curve.

Limiting cases: At the center (\(x = 0\)): \(B = \mu_0 I/(2R)\) — the maximum on-axis value. Far from the loop (\(x \gg R\)): \(B \approx \mu_0 IR^2/(2x^3) \propto 1/x^3\) — the dipole falloff, the same \(1/r^3\) dependence we found for the electric field far from an electric dipole in Chapter 22. The current loop IS a magnetic dipole.

Example: Fields from a Coil and a Wire

(A) A 50-turn coil (\(R = 0.10\ \text{m}\), \(I = 2.0\ \text{A}\)). At center: \(B = N\mu_0 I/(2R) = (50)(4\pi\times10^{-7})(2.0)/(0.20) = \boxed{0.63\ \text{mT}}\) — about 12× Earth’s field. A modest coil already dominates the local magnetic environment.

(B) A long wire (\(I = 5.0\ \text{A}\)) at \(r = 0.10\ \text{m}\): \(B = \mu_0 I/(2\pi r) = \boxed{10\ \mu\text{T}}\) — comparable to Earth’s field. At \(r = 0.050\ \text{m}\), \(B = 20\ \mu\text{T}\). The \(1/r\) dependence is linear, not quadratic.

28.6 — Ampère’s Law

The Magnetic Analog of Gauss’s Law

In Chapter 23, Gauss’s Law provided a powerful shortcut for calculating \(\vec{E}\) when symmetry cooperated. The magnetic analog is Ampère’s Law:

\[\boxed{\oint\vec{B}\cdot d\vec{\ell} = \mu_0 I_\text{enc}}\]

The line integral of \(\vec{B}\) around any closed Amperian loop equals \(\mu_0\) times the net current threading the loop. Like Gauss’s Law, always true but only useful when symmetry makes \(|\vec{B}|\) constant on the path.

Property Gauss’s Law (Ch 23) Ampère’s Law (Ch 28)
Integral type Surface (\(\oint\vec{E}\cdot d\vec{A}\)) Line (\(\oint\vec{B}\cdot d\vec{\ell}\))
Encloses Charge \(Q_\text{enc}\) Current \(I_\text{enc}\)
Constant \(\varepsilon_0\) (permittivity) \(\mu_0\) (permeability)
Useful when Symmetry \(\rightarrow\) \(E\) constant on surface Symmetry \(\rightarrow\) \(B\) constant on path

The Infinite Wire (Revisited)

A circular Amperian loop of radius \(r\) centered on the wire. By symmetry, \(\vec{B}\) is tangent and constant: \(B(2\pi r) = \mu_0 I\), giving \(B = \mu_0 I/(2\pi r)\). Confirms Biot-Savart in one line — the elegance of Ampère’s Law is that symmetry does the heavy lifting.

The Solenoid

A solenoid is a tightly wound coil, long compared to its diameter, producing a nearly uniform interior field and negligible exterior field. Choose a rectangular Amperian loop: one side of length \(L\) inside (parallel to axis), one outside (\(B \approx 0\)), two perpendicular sides (\(\vec{B}\perp d\vec{\ell}\)). Only the inside side contributes:

\[BL = \mu_0(nL)I \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad \boxed{B = \mu_0 nI} \qquad \text{(inside an ideal solenoid)}\]

where \(n = N/L_\text{total}\) is the number of turns per unit length.

The field depends only on \(n\) and \(I\) — not on position, radius, or length. The solenoid is the magnetic analog of the parallel-plate capacitor:

Parallel-Plate Capacitor (Ch 25) Ideal Solenoid (Ch 28)
Uniform \(E = \sigma/\varepsilon_0\) inside Uniform \(B = \mu_0 nI\) inside
\(E = 0\) outside \(B = 0\) outside
Energy density \(u_E = \frac{1}{2}\varepsilon_0 E^2\) Energy density \(u_B = B^2/(2\mu_0)\)

A toroid (solenoid bent into a doughnut) has \(B = \mu_0 NI/(2\pi r)\) inside — varying with \(r\), stronger near the inner wall — and \(B = 0\) outside.

*Personal note: The formula \(B = \mu_0 nI\) is the design equation for every MRI machine, particle accelerator, and electromagnetic relay. Need more field? Add more turns per meter or increase the current.

28.7 — Magnetic Flux and Gauss’s Law for Magnetism

Magnetic Flux

By analogy with electric flux (Ch 23), we define magnetic flux:

\[\boxed{\Phi_B = \int\vec{B}\cdot d\vec{A}} \qquad \text{For uniform } B: \quad \Phi_B = BA\cos\theta\]

The SI unit is the weber (Wb): \(1\ \text{Wb} = 1\ \text{T}\cdot\text{m}^2\).

Electric Flux (Ch 23) Magnetic Flux (Ch 28)
\(\Phi_E = \int\vec{E}\cdot d\vec{A}\) \(\Phi_B = \int\vec{B}\cdot d\vec{A}\)
Through closed surface: \(Q_\text{enc}/\varepsilon_0\) (can be \(\neq 0\)) Through closed surface: always \(= 0\)

Gauss’s Law for Magnetism

\[\boxed{\oint\vec{B}\cdot d\vec{A} = 0}\]

The net magnetic flux through any closed surface is always zero — every field line that enters must exit. This is Gauss’s Law for magnetism, one of Maxwell’s four equations. Cut a bar magnet in half \(\rightarrow\) two complete magnets, each with N and S poles. You can never isolate a single pole. Field lines inside the magnet run from S to N, closing the loops that run N to S outside.

This is the simplest of Maxwell’s four equations — and arguably the most profound. If a magnetic monopole were ever discovered, this equation would need a nonzero right-hand side, and Maxwell’s equations would become perfectly symmetric. The search continues.

28.8 — Summary

Key Concepts

  1. The magnetic field \(\vec{B}\) exerts a force on moving charges but not on stationary ones. SI unit: tesla (T).

  2. The magnetic force \(\vec{F} = q\vec{v}\times\vec{B}\) is always \(\perp\) to \(\vec{v}\) — it does no work, changing direction but never speed.

  3. A charge moving \(\perp\) to \(\vec{B}\) follows a circular orbit with \(r = mv/(|q|B)\) and frequency \(f = |q|B/(2\pi m)\), independent of speed.

  4. The force on a wire is \(\vec{F} = I\vec{L}\times\vec{B}\), with magnitude \(F = BIL\sin\theta\).

  5. A current loop has magnetic dipole moment \(\vec{\mu} = NIA\hat{n}\). Torque: \(\vec{\tau} = \vec{\mu}\times\vec{B}\); energy: \(U = -\vec{\mu}\cdot\vec{B}\) — structurally identical to the electric dipole (Ch 25).

  6. The Biot-Savart Law gives the field of a current element. Infinite wire: \(B = \mu_0 I/(2\pi r)\).

  7. Ampère’s Law: \(\oint\vec{B}\cdot d\vec{\ell} = \mu_0 I_\text{enc}\). Inside an ideal solenoid: \(B = \mu_0 nI\).

  8. Gauss’s Law for magnetism: \(\oint\vec{B}\cdot d\vec{A} = 0\) — magnetic field lines always form closed loops.

Looking Ahead

In Chapter 29, we discover what happens when magnetic fields change with time. Faraday’s Law tells us that a changing magnetic flux through a loop induces an EMF — voltage appears without any battery. This is the principle behind every generator, transformer, and wireless charging pad. Combined with Ampère’s Law and Maxwell’s displacement current (which you encountered in Chapter 31), Faraday’s Law closes the circle: changing \(\vec{B}\) creates \(\vec{E}\), and changing \(\vec{E}\) creates \(\vec{B}\). That mutual creation is the mechanism of electromagnetic waves — and the reason light exists.

Chapter 29 also introduces inductors, RL circuits, and LC oscillations — circuits that oscillate at \(\omega = 1/\sqrt{LC}\), converting energy between electric and magnetic fields in the same way EM waves convert energy between \(\vec{E}\) and \(\vec{B}\) in free space.

*In this chapter, we treated magnetic fields as static — created by steady currents and acting on moving charges. But the deepest physics lives in the dynamics: fields that change, propagate, and carry energy across empty space at the speed of light. Faraday’s Law is the door to that world.
